description: Make AI product videos and photos for beauty brands: texture close-ups, routine clips, and kit shots from one photo of your bottle or jar. Try it today.
h1: AI Product Videos and Photos for Beauty Brands, From Swatch to Shelf
lead: AI product videos and photos for beauty brands show the texture, the packaging, and where your product fits in a morning or evening routine, starting from one photo of your bottle, jar, or tube.
card: Texture close-ups, routine clips and kit shots from one photo of your bottle or jar.
intro: Show a cream’s texture in a separate swatch photo and place the bottle in a hand for scale. A routine scene can add context, while clear product-only photos still suit a product page or marketplace listing.

Pair a photo of your serum or balm with a sentence about the setting you picture: a marble vanity in soft morning light, toner pressed onto a cotton pad, a travel kit laid out on a folded towel. Videos can run 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds, vertical for TikTok and Reels or square for feeds. Every photo comes out square by default, a good fit for listings and carousel posts.

ideas.d: Put your product into a quick morning or night routine: cap off, a pump into the palm, back on the shelf. Vertical 9:16 fits Stories, Reels, and TikTok without awkward cropping.
If you sell a set, show the included pieces together in a square image. Lay them out in your upload photo so you can check the item count.
Place a moisturizer on a bathroom shelf, a lipstick in a makeup bag, or a sunscreen in a beach tote. Scenes like these give your gallery a sense of everyday use beyond the white background.

faq.q: Can I make before-and-after videos for a skincare product?
faq.a: We’d steer away from it for skin results. A generated face is not evidence of what your product does, and a visible change in skin can read as a promise. Show application, texture, and packaging instead, and leave claims about results out of your request and the claims you use in an ad.

faq.q: Will the video match my exact foundation or lipstick shade?
faq.a: Color comes from your photo and your wording, so shoot in daylight and name the shade plainly, like "warm beige liquid" or "brick red matte." If the tone still drifts, generate another version; the credit cost is shown before each one.

faq.q: Can I add my price or a promo code to the image?
faq.a: Type prices, promo codes, and product names on afterward in Canva or CapCut. Lettering made by AI can come out misspelled, so keep the image clean and add the words yourself.

faq.q: What kind of product photo should I upload for skincare?
faq.a: A straight-on shot with the label toward the camera, on a plain surface, with no hands or clutter in the frame. Glossy tubes and clear glass pick up glare, so shoot beside a window rather than using flash.

overview.h2: Show the formula, the finish, and the routine

items.t: Let the product answer the first questions
items.d: A bottle or jar photo establishes the pack. A close crop can show a serum, balm, or lipstick finish. Keep shade names and ingredient claims in product details your team has approved; generated imagery supplies context.

items.t: Build a small set of useful views
items.d: Use one result for the listing, one for a vanity or travel scene, and one short clip for a pump, dropper, or opened compact. That sequence gives shoppers context without pretending a generated face proves a skincare result.
Place the bottle, tube, or jar upright with the front label toward the camera. Include the full cap and base so the package shape is not guessed.
Use a window or diffused lamp beside the product instead of direct flash. Rotate glossy plastic and clear glass until the label is readable and hot spots are small.
For a cream, balm, powder, or lipstick, add a separate swatch or texture photo. A packshot cannot reveal a finish that never appears in the upload.
Lay out all bottles, minis, pouches, or tools for a bundle shot. Keep the pieces separated enough that the final count is easy to check.

items.t: Keep claims out of the scene
items.d: Describe a bathroom shelf, mirror tray, or travel pouch rather than an implied medical outcome. Add approved claims later in the channel where your team controls the wording.
An amber serum bottle beside a white sink, cap off, one dropper hovering above the back of a hand, with soft morning window light.
Three lipstick swatches on a warm ivory card beside the closed tubes, cropped close enough to show the different finishes.
A cleanser, toner, and moisturizer lined up on a small stone vanity with a folded towel and no extra brand marks.
A sunscreen tube and two minis inside an open canvas toiletry pouch on a hotel bathroom counter, labels facing out.
Use a square photo for a gallery, then pair it with a close detail of the finish or applicator.
A vertical 9:16 clip can follow one simple action, while 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, and 3:4 frames cover other placements.
A photo costs 24 credits. Six-, ten-, fifteen-, and thirty-second videos cost 24, 40, 60, and 120 credits; the charge is shown before you run the job.
Review commercial-use and watermark information in the [FAQ](/faq) before publishing.

after_download.h2: Finish the beauty asset after download

items.d: Compare cap shape, label placement, shade, and item count with the real package before publishing.
Place price, shade name, promotion dates, and approved claims in Canva, CapCut, or your ad editor so every character is exact.
AIVideosUGC does not add voiceover, music, or captions; add shade names and product details in your publishing tool after download.

fit.h2: A good fit for beauty products

good.d: Bottles, jars, tubes, compacts, and boxed sets with a clear front view.
Creams, powders, balms, drops, and swatches that you can photograph separately.
Products that benefit from a shelf, vanity, travel, or gift-set context.

not_ideal.d: Do not use a generated image as the sole proof of a precise color match; compare with a real swatch.
